[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in mathematics i = 0, i < n and i = i + 1 are equations or constraints that hold at the same time (and i = i + 1 is nonsense). In Java they are three actions run at different moments: init once, test before each pass, update after each pass.
[1] misconception (M) -> PreIncrementBeforeLoop: wrong rule: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass. Right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.
[2] misconception (M) -> OffByOneBound: wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> PreIncrementBeforeLoop: Applies the init-test-update rule (LT) unevenly: updates before the body on some passes, skips the test or the update on a pass, or re-runs the init. (here mixing in: "++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass")
[4] misconception (M) -> InfiniteLoopUnnoticed: wrong rule: a condition that never goes false still terminates. Right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.
[5] misconception (M) -> DoubleLoopIndexCount: wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
[6] misconception (M) -> IdiomOverridesCode: wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
[7] misconception (M) -> LoopHeaderIsEquations: wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. Right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.
[8] misconception (M) -> ForLoopPartSkipped: wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.
[9] misconception (M) -> ForUpdateBeforeBody: wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. Right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.
[10] misconception (M) -> LoopUpdateChangesDirection: wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. Right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.
[11] misconception (M) -> LoopStepAlwaysOne: wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). Right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

[0] names_the_element (N): Loop control is the init / continuation condition / increment scheme on an index variable that decides how many passes a loop makes and with which values.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Initialize an index variable, test a loop-continuation condition on it before each pass, and increment it as the last action of each pass; for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) packages the three. Choosing the loop: for when the passes are counted by an index, while when the loop runs until a condition changes, do-while when the body must run at least once; any one can be rewritten as another, so choose the clearest.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): init (once) -> test -> body -> update -> test -> body -> update ... -> test false -> exit.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The number of passes and the values seen follow from the three parts: for (int i = 0; i <= N; i++) makes N+1 passes with i = 0..N; with i < N it makes N passes; i += 2 visits every second value.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One update changes only the loop variable, by exactly the rule written (i++ adds 1, i = i - 4 subtracts 4); one test reads it and returns true or false without changing it.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): All three control parts act on the loop variable: the init sets it, the condition tests it, the update changes it.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): The for header is exactly the three control slots, separated by semicolons; the body runs after the test and before the update.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): The update i = i + 1 is usually written i++ (or i += k for other steps); as a whole update statement ++i and i++ are equivalent.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): A loop is infinite when the update never moves the variable toward making the condition false (e.g. condition i > 3 with update i = i + 1).
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): The continuation condition fixes the number of iterations, so a sharper bound (i <= n/i instead of i < n) can make a program dramatically faster.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): The initialization and the condition of a loop fix how many times it runs; one wrong bound makes it run once too many or too few.
[6] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: counter-controlled loop - the loop variable is a stepper that walks a predictable sequence of values (0..N-1, 1..N, every 2nd value) and fixes the number of passes in advance.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> PreIncrementBeforeLoop: Changing < to <= adds one pass; starting at 1 instead of 0 removes one; doubling the step halves the passes; reversing init and bound with i-- visits the same values in reverse order (and still processes the same set only if both ends are adjusted).
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The number of passes is fixed by the init, the test and the update together. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Wrong start value, < vs <=, a wrong step, or an extra update of the counter in the body (or outside the loop): the loop runs too few or too many passes (off by one, or skips values).
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use explicit init/test/update control when the passes are counted or follow a fixed step; when the number of passes depends on data computed in the body, control the loop by that data (a while condition) instead.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The update must move the loop variable toward making the condition false. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: An update in the wrong direction or a condition that the update cannot falsify (e.g. i > 3 with i++, or i != 10 with i += 3): infinite loop.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Do not control a loop by an equality test on double values. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: for (double x = 0.0; x < 1.0; x += 0.1): after ten additions x is 0.9999999999999999, so the loop makes 11 passes instead of the intended 10.

A do-while loop has the same control parts as a while loop (the variable set before, the condition, the update in the body); only the test is moved after the body.
The for header is exactly the three control slots, and the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
The loop update i = i + 1 comes first; ++ (and +=) are then introduced as shorthand for that update.
A loop is infinite when its update never moves the condition towards false.
break with a label leaves the labelled outer loop, not only the innermost one.
The loop condition decides how many iterations run, so a better test (i <= n/i instead of i < n) makes the program much faster.
The initialization and the condition of a loop fix how many times it runs; one wrong bound makes it run once too many or too few.
The init, condition and update all act on the loop variable: the init sets it, the condition tests it, the update changes it.

A while loop has the same three control parts as a for loop, written in other places: the index set before the loop, the loop-continuation condition in the header, and the update as the last statement of the body.
